Pre-requisites 4 1. Steps to Configure the Private Node (Procify IDE) 5 2. Start the Procify IDE server 19 3. Start your Procify IDE Application 20

Application url: https://<domain_Name>p6/<Landscape>/index.html Note: URL should be applied according to the server in which the Procify IDE will be set up. Please check whether the URL is accessible in your browser with a valid SSL certificate. If it is not accessible then contact the Admin team. You should have the Procify IDE Installer file (.exe). This installer will change the node modules' global installation path and if you are having any modules installed globally, please reinstall again after this installation is completed. Remove the node path which is set in the user environment variables. Path: C:\Users\< user profile >\AppData\Roaming\npm

Step 1 - Add Admin Credentials Double click the installer file (.exe) and enter the Administrator credentials to start the installation. [For Admin credentials, please contact Admin team] Step 2 - Accept License agreement Accept the license agreement and click on next. Step 3 - Select Procify IDE Setup Location Select the folder where you want to create the workspace for your procify IDE setup and click on next. NOTE: By default the destination folder will be “C:\Procify\workspace”. Please change the destination folder to any editable drive (example: D or E). Until and unless you are logged in as an administrator user, you will not be able to create or edit any files that are present in C drive. In the below image it shows the destination folder as D:\workspace\trunkqa where instead of trunkqa put a name by which you will be able to understand which server you are creating your Procify IDE setup. In case you are using this Procify IDE installer multiple times then change the destination folder accordingly. Click on Next. Step 4 - Add Server Information A new Dialog will appear asking for server information. Enter all the credential details in the required fields. The server details include the following: Credentials Credential Details Application index url This url will keep changing based on the domain and landscape you use it for. For example: https://<domain_Name>Klarion/u/c/V1/<Landscape>/fs/index.html User Id This is the Procify user credentials used to login to the application. Password This is the password used to login to the application. Fill in all the details and click on Next. Step 5 - Select Additional Task A new dialog will appear as shown in the image below, the default checkbox will be checked for “Create a desktop shortcut”. Then click on next. Note: If you do not want to create any shortcut on your desktop screen then uncheck the box and proceed. Step 6 - Install Procify IDE file After that, the “Ready to Install” page will appear. Click on install. This step will take some time to load. Kindly, wait until the process is completed. ![][image6] Step 7 - Accept the Folder Authentication Query After installation, the workspace folder will open in Visual Studio Code. Click on “Yes, I trust the author Trust folder and enable all features” to proceed to the next step. ![][image7] Now in the VS code, IDE setup will be in process. It will automatically trigger a command npm run kloServerStart. This will download all the required files and it will take some time, kindly wait till the process is complete. ![][image8] Once the above process is completed, it will automatically open the Repository. Here you checkout the Apps by selecting those apps and click on checkout. ![][image9] After clicking on the checkout it will download the App files from the server to the workspace. ![][image10] Once the apps checkout is done it will show the ‘Files Checkouted Successful‘ message. Step 8 - Accept the Folder Authentication Query Once the above process is completed, close the VS code instance. Then double click on the Procify IDE desktop shortcut and it will open your workspace folder in the VS code. If you opted not to create the Procify IDE desktop shortcut, then go to the destination folder you have provided during the start of the installation and open that folder in vs code by following the below steps: First open the workspace folder in the command prompt (In the file path, type cmd and press enter). Then type code . and enter, it will open your workspace folder in VS code. Click on “Yes, I trust the authors Trust folder and enable all features” to proceed to the next step. ![][image7]

Developer Level 2 — Advanced Track Enhancing the Customer Complaints Application This track does not build a new application. Every session goes back into the SAME Customer Complaints app built in Developer Level 1, and layers a new advanced capability onto it — the same end-to-end build approach used in the Level 1 guide. Prerequisite: Developer Level 1 completion is mandatory. Proposed dates are placeholders (one session per working day, starting Mon 07 Sep 2026) — confirm actual start date and cadence.

Developer Level 1 was built as an end-to-end project: one real application — the Customer Complaints Application — built up session by session. This Level 2 guide follows the same approach: no new application is created. Every session below re-opens the entities, pages, entity files, and controllers already built in Level 1 and extends them with an advanced capability, so trainees see how real applications evolve rather than practicing features in isolation. Topics are drawn from the Training Topics sheet, filtered to entries tagged “Developer Level 2,” and mapped onto concrete enhancements of the existing app. Tool names use the current naming glossary, with legacy names noted where relevant.

Sessions must be taken in order — each session's steps assume the previous session's enhancement is already in place, exactly as in the Level 1 guide. Session Date Topic Area Application Enhancement Session 1 Mon, 07 Sep 2026 Advanced BOL & Data Modelling Network Modes — Offline-Ready Properties · Sort Order & Entity Index · Entity Rules — Auto-Escalation on Update · Query Rules — Role-Based Field Masking · BOL Transaction — Close Complaint with Feedback Session 2 Tue, 08 Sep 2026 Advanced Page Builder & Client-Side Debugging Embedded Section — Complaint Timeline · Advanced kloControls · TransNode onArrive & navigateId · Server-Side Debugging & Auto Update Data Session 3 Wed, 09 Sep 2026 Security, Permissions & Data Access Design-Time Permissions · Row Wise Auth · Data Access Rules & User Access Summary · Role Permissions (Runtime) & Permission Logs Session 4 Thu, 10 Sep 2026 Offline, Middleware & Bulk Data Local Archive · Initial Downloads · Middleware — Device & SAP · KloSectionXlsx — Bulk Customer Import Session 5 Fri, 11 Sep 2026 Workflows, Scheduling & Notifications Escalation Approval Workflow · Scheduler — Nightly SLA Sweep · Notifications · deeplink & Banner Session 6 Mon, 14 Sep 2026 Reporting — Charts & Pivot Modeller kloChart — Status Breakdown · Advanced Chart — TAT Trend · Pivot Modeller Session 7 Tue, 15 Sep 2026 Monitoring & Troubleshooting Scheduler & Log Monitoring · Notification & Queue Monitoring · APK/IPA & Query Console Session 8 Wed, 16 Sep 2026 App Management, Branding & Deployment App Inheritance & Modification · Customer Branding · Git Repo & Active Sessions · App Migration to QA

Configure Network Modes so offline-relevant properties sync correctly to field devices. Apply Sort Order and an Entity Index to d_complaints for performance and predictable ordering. Extend the existing Entity Rules with a new auto-escalation rule. Extend the existing Query Rules with role-based field masking. Build a BOL Transaction that commits two entities atomically. What This Session Builds On Developer Level 1 (Sessions 1–5) built d_complaints with its properties, one Entity Rule (onCreateComplaint) and one Query Rule (beforeQ) on q_complaints. This session does not start a new entity — it goes back into the same d_complaints and q_complaints files and adds the advanced BOL capabilities on top.

A field IT Team member on a tablet needs complaint status and priority visible even with no signal, while internal notes stay server-side only. Meanwhile complaints are quietly sailing past SLA with no auto-flag, and a support rep spots that anyone on the IT Team can see a customer's full contact details in the list — details they never needed for their job.

Not every property should sync to a field device the same way. Configure Network Mode per property on d_complaints. # Action Detail 1 Open properties Procify Data Studio → d_complaints → Properties tab. 2 Restrict remark Set Network Mode = Online Only on remark — internal notes should not be cached on IT Team field devices. 3 Always sync core fields Set Network Mode = Always on complaint_id, s_status, priority so they remain visible even when the device is offline. 4 Save & update schema Save, then Update Schema, and confirm no errors.
documents.s: Part A — Network Modes — Offline-Ready Properties

documents.t: The complaints list currently has no defined default order and no index for the fields it is filtered on most. # Action Detail 1 Set Sort Order On priority: custom order CRITICAL > HIGH > MEDIUM > LOW. On created_on: DESCENDING as the secondary sort. 2 Create Entity Index Entity Index tab → Add → ID: idx_complaint_status_priority — fields: s_status, priority. 3 Update Schema Update Schema and verify the index is listed under the entity's Test → Data Browser diagnostics.
documents.s: Part B — Sort Order & Entity Index

documents.t: Reopen the same d_complaints.ts file from Level 1 Session 5 and add a second rule alongside onCreateComplaint. # Action Detail 1 Register the rule Rule tab → Add → Event Type: On Update | Channel: Always on Server | Clazz: this | Invocation Method: checkEscalation. 2 Implement checkEscalation If s_status is OPEN or INPROCESS and (today − created_on) > 3 days, set is_escalated = true. 3 Test Backdate a test record's created_on in Data Browser to 4 days ago, save, and confirm is_escalated flips to true.
documents.s: Part C — Entity Rules — Auto-Escalation on Update

documents.t: Extend q_complaints.ts — the same file where beforeQ was written in Level 1 Session 4 — with an afterQ rule. # Action Detail 1 Add afterQ Event Type: After Query. In the handler, if the requesting role is IT_TEAM, replace customer contact fields in each result row with ‘•••’. 2 Test as IT Team Log in as it_<prid> — confirm customer contact fields are masked in the list. 3 Test as Manager Log in as mgr_<prid> — confirm the same fields show full data.
documents.s: Part D — Query Rules — Role-Based Field Masking

documents.t: Combine a status update and a new voice record into one atomic operation. # Action Detail 1 Create the transaction Data Studio → new BOL Transaction Tx_CloseWithFeedback, covering d_complaints (update s_status = CLOSED) and d_complaint_voices (create feedback record). 2 Wire the button Add a ‘Close with Feedback’ action on s_detail_header that commits both TransNodes through this transaction. 3 Test atomicity Force the voice record to fail validation (e.g. leave it blank) and confirm the status change also rolls back — not just the voice record. Session 1 Checkpoint ✔ Network Modes verified in an offline emulation for at least 3 properties. ✔ s_complaints defaults to priority order; idx_complaint_status_priority exists and is used. ✔ checkEscalation rule fires correctly on a backdated test record. ✔ afterQ masks customer fields for IT_TEAM but not for Manager. ✔ Tx_CloseWithFeedback commits both entities together or rolls back together. Enhancement delivered: Extends the existing d_complaints / q_complaints files from Level 1 (not a new entity) with offline sync control, performance indexing, automatic SLA escalation, field-level data masking by role, and an atomic close-with-feedback commit.
documents.s: Part E — BOL Transaction — Close Complaint with Feedback

documents.t: Build a reusable Embedded Section and use it on two different pages. Add Advanced kloControls (rating, file uploader) to the detail screen. Configure TransNode onArrive and navigateId behaviour. Debug the Session 1 server-side rule using Server-Side Debugging. Enable Auto Update Data so the Manager's list refreshes without manual action. What This Session Builds On p_complaints was built manually in Level 1 Session 2 and styled in Session 6; p_complaint_dashboard was built in Session 5. Both existing pages are extended here — no new page is created from scratch.

A Manager opens a complaint and has to hunt across screens to see whether this customer has complained before. A rep marks a complaint resolved but there's no way to capture how satisfied the customer actually was, or attach a photo of a damaged product without emailing it separately.

Build one timeline section and reuse it in two places. # Action Detail 1 Create the section New section s_complaint_timeline (screenType: timeline) bound to a TransNode combining voices and status-change history. 2 Embed in detail In pa_comp_details, add a new section, mark it Embedded, and point its source to s_complaint_timeline. 3 Reuse on dashboard Add the same embedded section to p_complaint_dashboard as a ‘Recent Activity’ panel — confirming true cross-page reuse.
documents.s: Part A — Embedded Section — Complaint Timeline

documents.t: Add two controls that were not covered in Level 1's basic control set. # Action Detail 1 Add kloRating On s_detail_header, add a kloRating control bound to a new transient property t_satisfaction_score, visible only when s_status = CLOSED. 2 Add kloFileUploader On the attachments section, add kloFileUploader bound to the d_complaints_attachment relation built in Level 1. 3 Full Preview Confirm the rating control only appears on closed complaints and the uploader stores a file record correctly.

Make the detail screen smarter about what loads automatically and where links resolve to. # Action Detail 1 Configure onArrive On the detail TransNode, set onArrive to auto-load the 5 most recent related voices — no extra click required. 2 Configure navigateId On the ticket_id link control, set navigateId so it always resolves to pa_complaint_details, whether clicked from p_complaints or the dashboard's embedded timeline. 3 Test both entry points Click a complaint from the main list, then from the dashboard timeline — confirm both land on the same detail area correctly populated.

Debug the rule written in Session 1 and make the Manager's grid self-refreshing. # Action Detail 1 Attach debugger Set a breakpoint inside checkEscalation in VS Code and attach to the running Private Node. 2 Step through Trigger a save on a test complaint and step through the rule execution line by line. 3 Enable auto refresh On s_complaints, set Auto Update Data = true with a 30-second interval. 4 Verify Create a complaint as Employee in one browser tab; confirm it appears in the Manager's grid within 30 seconds without a manual refresh. Session 2 Checkpoint ✔ s_complaint_timeline renders correctly on both p_complaints and p_complaint_dashboard. ✔ kloRating and kloFileUploader function as specified. ✔ onArrive auto-loads voices; navigateId resolves correctly from both entry points. ✔ Breakpoint debugging confirmed inside checkEscalation. ✔ Manager's grid auto-refreshes within 30 seconds of a new complaint being created. Enhancement delivered: Adds a reusable complaint-history timeline, a satisfaction rating and attachment capture on resolution, smarter auto-loading/navigation, and a self-refreshing Manager grid — all on the existing pages built in Level 1.
documents.s: Part D — Server-Side Debugging & Auto Update Data

documents.t: Enforce CRUD restrictions server-side using design-time Permissions. Restrict IT Team visibility to their own team's complaints using Row Wise Auth. Scope customer data by region using Data Access Rules. Audit a user's effective access using User Access Summary. Grant, use, and revoke a temporary elevated Role Permission, and confirm it in Permission Logs. What This Session Builds On Level 1 Session 7 hid or disabled buttons per role using Vienable — a UI-level control only. This session enforces the same rules at the platform/security level so they hold even if a user calls the API directly.

An IT Team member who left last month still has delete rights if they call the API directly, even though the button is hidden in the UI. A regional manager can see every customer's complaints nationwide instead of just their region, and after an override was granted during an incident, nobody can say who approved it or when it was revoked.

Configure real CRUD restrictions, not just hidden buttons. # Action Detail 1 Configure Employee Employee role: Create + Read only. 2 Configure Manager Manager role: Create + Read + Update + Delete. 3 Configure IT Team IT Team role: Read + Update only. 4 Test server-side block Log in as emp_<prid> and confirm Delete is blocked even if attempted outside the hidden button (e.g. via a direct API call).

Restrict IT Team to only the complaints assigned to their own team. # Action Detail 1 Configure the rule Row Wise Auth on d_complaints: IT_TEAM role only receives rows where responsible_team = current user's team. 2 Test Log in as it_<prid> — confirm only assigned complaints appear, even via direct navigation to a different complaint's URL.

Scope customer master data regionally and verify it. # Action Detail 1 Create the rule New Data Access Rule scoping d_customers by region. 2 Assign to Manager Assign the rule to mgr_<prid> for their region. 3 Verify with User Access Summary Open User Access Summary for mgr_<prid> and confirm the rule and effective permissions are listed correctly.
documents.s: Part C — Data Access Rules & User Access Summary

documents.t: Simulate an incident requiring temporary elevated access, then audit it. # Action Detail 1 Grant temporary access Create a runtime Role Permission override allowing IT_TEAM_LEAD to Delete during an incident. 2 Use and revoke Apply, test the elevated Delete, then revoke the override. 3 Audit in Permission Logs Confirm both the grant and the revoke appear in Permission Logs with timestamp and actor. Session 3 Checkpoint ✔ CRUD restrictions enforced server-side for all 3 roles. ✔ IT Team row-level filtering confirmed, including via direct URL access. ✔ Data Access Rule created, assigned, and confirmed via User Access Summary. ✔ Temporary Role Permission granted, used, revoked, and fully audited in Permission Logs. Enhancement delivered: Replaces Level 1's UI-only button hiding (Vienable) with rules enforced at the platform/security level, restricts IT Team visibility to assigned complaints, scopes customer data by region, and closes the audit gap on temporary access.
documents.s: Part D — Role Permissions (Runtime) & Permission Logs

documents.t: Enable offline access to assigned complaints for field IT Team users via Local Archive. Reduce first-login sync payload using Initial Downloads. Push closed complaints to an external SAP system via Middleware. Bulk-import customer master data using KloSectionXlsx. What This Session Builds On The application has only worked online through Sessions 1–3. This session makes it usable by IT Team members working onsite without connectivity, and adds a bulk-data path for customer onboarding.

An IT Team technician visiting a customer site with no signal can't pull up the complaint they're there to resolve. Every login re-downloads the full complaint history instead of just what's assigned, closed complaints aren't reaching the SAP billing system automatically, and onboarding 20 new customers means entering each one by hand.

Keep a working slice of data on the device for offline use. # Action Detail 1 Configure archive scope Local Archive on d_complaints and d_complaint_voices for the IT_TEAM role — retain the last 30 days of assigned complaints on-device. 2 Test offline On a device/emulator, disconnect network and confirm assigned complaints and their voice history are still viewable.

Reduce what gets pulled on first login. # Action Detail 1 Configure the download set Only OPEN/INPROCESS complaints assigned to the logging-in IT Team user are included in the first sync — not full history. 2 Verify Time a fresh login before and after the change and confirm a smaller payload.

Integrate with an external billing system. # Action Detail 1 Configure the channel New Middleware channel that pushes CLOSED complaints to an external SAP endpoint for billing reconciliation. 2 Test Close a test complaint and confirm the outbound payload appears in the middleware queue.

Add Excel-based bulk operations to the customer master entity. # Action Detail 1 Add to d_customers Attach KloSectionXlsx to the customer section, enabling bulk Excel upload/download. 2 Bulk import Prepare a sample sheet of 20 customers and import via the section. 3 Verify Confirm all 20 records land correctly in Data Browser. Session 4 Checkpoint ✔ IT Team can view assigned complaints and voice history fully offline. ✔ Initial download payload measurably reduced and verified. ✔ One closed complaint confirmed pushed to the SAP middleware queue. ✔ 20 customers successfully bulk-imported via KloSectionXlsx. Enhancement delivered: Makes the app usable in the field without connectivity, shrinks the first-login sync payload, automates the SAP billing hand-off on closure, and adds bulk customer onboarding.
documents.s: Part D — KloSectionXlsx — Bulk Customer Import

documents.t: Route escalated complaints through a Manager approval Workflow. Add a nightly Scheduled Task as a server-side safety net for SLA breaches. Notify the right people by Email, SMS, and In-App at the right moments. Deep-link notification emails directly into the relevant complaint. Configure an app-wide Banner for planned maintenance. What This Session Builds On Session 1 added a server-side is_escalated flag. This session adds the human workflow and communication layer that reacts to it.

A complaint sits open for a week past SLA with no one following up, because there's no approval step and no nightly check catching it. A customer is never told their complaint was resolved unless someone remembers to call, and a support email can't deep-link straight to the complaint it's about.

Give escalation a human decision point. # Action Detail 1 Build the workflow When is_escalated becomes true, route an approval task to the Manager to confirm reassignment of responsible_team. 2 Test Trigger escalation on a test complaint and confirm the Manager receives the task in Pending Approvals.

Add a server-side safety net independent of individual saves. # Action Detail 1 Create the task Scheduled Task that runs nightly, re-checking all OPEN/INPROCESS complaints against the 3-day SLA rule from Session 1. 2 Run manually and verify Trigger once via Running Tasks and confirm overdue complaints are correctly flagged.
documents.s: Part B — Scheduler — Nightly SLA Sweep

documents.t: Close the communication loop for assignment and resolution. # Action Detail 1 Assignment email Email notification to responsible_team the moment a complaint is assigned. 2 Resolution in-app alert In-App notification to the originating Employee when status changes to CLOSED. 3 Verify delivery Trigger both scenarios and confirm delivery in Notification History.

Make notifications actionable and announce planned downtime. # Action Detail 1 Configure deeplink The assignment email's ‘View Complaint’ link opens directly to the correct complaint detail screen. 2 Configure Banner App-wide banner announcing a planned maintenance window, visible to all roles for 24 hours. Session 5 Checkpoint ✔ Escalation approval task correctly routed to and actionable by the Manager. ✔ Nightly scheduler flags overdue complaints on a manual run. ✔ Assignment email and resolution in-app alert both confirmed delivered in Notification History. ✔ Deeplink opens the exact correct complaint; banner visible to all 3 roles. Enhancement delivered: Adds a human approval step on escalation, a nightly check independent of individual saves, closes the communication loop on assignment/resolution, and makes notifications actionable.

Replace static dashboard tiles with a live kloChart. Build an advanced TAT trend chart over a rolling 30-day window. Build a Pivot Modeller report for cross-team, cross-type analysis. What This Session Builds On Level 1 Session 5 built p_complaint_dashboard with static status-count tiles fed by status_count_query. This session replaces and extends those same tiles with real charts.

A Manager glances at the dashboard and sees numbers that were already stale this morning, with no way to see the SLA trend over the last month or drill into which team is falling behind — only static totals.

Turn the existing tile counts into a live chart. # Action Detail 1 Add the chart Add a kloChart bar chart to p_complaint_dashboard bound to the existing status_count_query TransNode. 2 Cross-check and replace Verify the chart's counts match the old static tiles, then remove the tiles.

Add a second, more advanced chart tracking service-level performance. # Action Detail 1 Build the query New query aggregating actual_tat vs standard_tat by week for the last 30 days. 2 Configure the chart Advanced line chart with two series (actual vs standard) and custom axis formatting.
documents.s: Part B — Advanced Chart — TAT Trend

documents.t: Give Managers a drillable cross-tab report. # Action Detail 1 Build the pivot Rows = complaint_type, Columns = responsible_team, Values = count of complaints, Filter = current month. 2 Publish & verify Publish to the EAM Portal and confirm a Manager can drill into a specific cell to see the underlying records. Session 6 Checkpoint ✔ Static dashboard tiles fully replaced by a live kloChart with matching counts. ✔ TAT trend chart renders 30 days of actual-vs-standard data. ✔ Pivot report published to EAM Portal and drill-down verified. Enhancement delivered: Replaces static dashboard tiles with live, trend-aware reporting and adds a drillable cross-tab view for Managers.

Diagnose a simulated scheduler failure end-to-end using platform monitoring tools. Confirm notification delivery and resolve a stuck offline sync record. Confirm the SAP middleware payload was processed via Legacy Queue Monitoring. Trace a native control rendering issue on a built APK. Independently verify dashboard numbers using Query Console. What This Session Builds On The app is feature-complete after Sessions 1–6 (automation, offline sync, integrations, reporting). This session is entirely about operating and troubleshooting what was built, not adding new features.

The nightly SLA sweep silently failed last night and nobody noticed until complaints started piling up unflagged. A customer insists they never got a resolution notification, and there's no way to check; finance says a closed complaint never showed up in SAP and nobody can tell whether it's stuck or lost.

Break the Session 5 scheduler on purpose, then find and fix it. # Action Detail 1 Simulate a failure Introduce a bad condition into the nightly SLA-sweep task and trigger it. 2 Observe the failure Confirm the failure appears in Scheduler Monitoring and Task History. 3 Trace the root cause Find the underlying error in Google Logs. 4 Fix and re-run Correct the task and confirm success via Running Tasks.

Confirm the Session 4 and 5 integrations are actually working end-to-end. # Action Detail 1 Verify notifications Check Notification History for the assignment/resolution messages from Session 5 — confirm delivered status. 2 Diagnose a stuck sync Simulate a stuck offline record on Server Queue / Mobile Sync Queue for an IT Team device from Session 4, and resolve it. 3 Check the SAP channel Review Legacy Queue Monitoring to confirm the Session 4 closed-complaint payload to SAP was processed.

Trace a native rendering issue and cross-verify reporting data. # Action Detail 1 Build and test the APK Build a debug APK including the kloRating control from Session 2. 2 Debug if needed If the control fails to render natively, use APK/IPA debugging tools to trace the issue. 3 Cross-verify dashboard data Use Query Console to independently confirm the raw row counts behind the Session 6 dashboard charts. Session 7 Checkpoint ✔ Simulated scheduler failure diagnosed via Scheduler Monitoring + Google Logs and resolved. ✔ Notification delivery confirmed; one stuck sync record identified and resolved. ✔ SAP payload confirmed processed in Legacy Queue Monitoring. ✔ APK rendering issue for kloRating traced (fixed or root-caused). ✔ Dashboard chart numbers cross-verified against raw data via Query Console. Enhancement delivered: Shifts the training from building features to operating and troubleshooting everything Sessions 1–6 put in place.

Create a client-specific child flavor using App Inheritance. Customize the child flavor without touching the base app via App Modification. Apply Customer Branding to the login page, menus, and headers. Version-control all Level 2 code in a Git repo. Migrate the fully enhanced application to QA and confirm every enhancement survived. What This Session Builds On The base Customer Complaints app is now feature-rich after Sessions 1–7. This final session prepares it for a real client rollout — a branded, inherited child flavor, migrated to QA.

The business is onboarding a new client, Acme, who needs their own complaint categories and branded login screen without touching the shared base app every other client depends on. Before go-live, someone has to confirm a departed developer's session is revoked and that the whole app still works correctly once it's moved to QA.

Create a client-specific variant without duplicating the whole app. # Action Detail 1 Create the child flavor New flavor customer_complaints_acme_<prid> inheriting from the base application. 2 Override safely Use App Modification to override complaint_type values for Acme's business categories, without changing the base flavor.

Make the child flavor visually distinct. # Action Detail 1 Update login/registration Modify the index file for the Acme child flavor with Acme's logo and welcome text. 2 Apply CSS Style menus and headers to match Acme's brand colors, scoped to .procify__customer_complaints_acme_<prid>.

Clean up before go-live. # Action Detail 1 Push code to Git Push all entity rules, controller code, and CSS written across Sessions 1–8 into a Git repo. 2 Review sessions Check Active Sessions for the app and revoke any stale developer sessions before go-live.
documents.s: Part C — Git Repo & Active Sessions

documents.t: Ship the enhanced application and prove every feature survived the move. # Action Detail 1 Release the flavor Release the Acme child flavor. 2 Migrate Run App Migration (Transport) from DEV to QA. 3 Full smoke test On QA, verify: escalation rule (S1), embedded timeline (S2), permissions/row-level auth (S3), offline sync (S4), workflow + notifications (S5), dashboard charts (S6), and Acme branding (S8) all work correctly. Session 8 Checkpoint ✔ Acme child flavor created, visually distinct, and functionally overridden without touching the base app. ✔ All Level 2 code version-controlled in Git. ✔ Stale developer sessions reviewed and revoked. ✔ Application migrated to QA with every Session 1–8 enhancement verified working end-to-end. Enhancement delivered: Delivers a branded, client-specific flavor without touching the shared base app, and proves every Session 1–8 enhancement survives the move to QA.
documents.s: Part D — App Migration to QA

Training Procedure Welcome to the Procify Developer Training. This section explains the overall structure of the course, how sessions are designed, and what is expected of you as a trainee. Read this before starting Session 1. Course Structure — 8 Sessions​ The training spans 8 sessions. Each session introduces a new layer of the platform — starting with setup and ending with publishing a fully working application. Sessions must be taken in order; each one builds directly on the previous. Session Topic Session 1 Platform Setup & Account Management Session 2 BOL — Entity Fundamentals & Initial Pages Session 3 Entity Configuration (Relations, Object Types, Status, ID Series) Session 4 Value Helps & Queries Session 5 BOL Logic & Validations with dashboard creation Session 6 Bindings, Navigation & Styling Session 7 Controllers & Client-Side Behaviour Session 8 Menu Configuration & App Management, Versioning & Publishing The Learn-by-Building Approach​ This training does not teach concepts in isolation. You will build one real application — a Customer complaint system — across all 89 sessions. Every concept is introduced exactly when you need it to make the next part of that application work. Why this matters for you You will always know WHY you are doing each step, not just HOW. By Session 8 you will have a working application demonstrating every major platform capability. The application grows session by session — if you miss a step it will affect later sessions. When you encounter a similar situation on a real project, you will have a concrete reference point from training.

Attend each session with the previous session's assignment completed and verified. Follow steps in this guide during hands-on time — do not skip ahead. Ask questions during the Review & Q&A phase, not during the trainer demonstration. The Application You Will Build This training guide uses a REAL application: the Customer complaints Application. You are not building a demo — you are building a production-ready application for delivery personnel. Every concept taught in every session is applied directly to build this application. By Session 9 you will have a fully working, published Delivery Agent Application.

Session Objectives​ By the end of this session, we will be able to: Understand the platform architecture. Create an application in the Workspace Hub. Define application roles and understand system vs. application roles. Create user accounts and assign them to an application with the correct role. Use Team Groups (User collections) to bundle multiple users and assign them to an application in a single, bulk step. Understands the role of data studio and page builder in application creation. ⚠ Why this session comes first The App you create today is built across ALL 9 sessions — treat it carefully. The Roles you define today are referenced in Session 5 (Validations) and Session 9 (Publishing access). The Users you create today are the test personas you will use to verify every screen built in Sessions 2–8. Part A — Understanding the Customer complaint Application​ Before touching any tool, you need a clear picture of the application you are building. Read this section carefully — every configuration decision in Sessions 1– traces back to this Business Requirement Document. Application Purpose​ The Customer Complaints Application is a solution designed to manage customer complaints end-to-end across three personas: • Log and track customer complaints with full lifecycle management. • Route complaints from Employee → Manager → Responsible Team. • Manage complaint line items, voice records, and file attachments. • Monitor escalations, SLA (TAT), and resolution timelines. • Provide dashboards per role so every user sees what they need. Application Roles — Three Personas​ This application defines exactly three application roles, each mapped to a Procify role-rollup level for viewable and UI-Auth controls: Role ID Business Name Procify Role Rollup Employee Complaint Creator Owner (s_role_rollup = 10) Manager Complaint Assignor Supervisor (s_role_rollup = 20) Responsible Team Issue Resolver Reviewer (s_role_rollup = 30) 📘 Role Precedence Rule Precedence is a number. Lower = higher priority. Employee: precedence 3, Manager: precedence 2, ResponsibleTeam: precedence 1. This means if a user has multiple roles, the lower-precedence number overrides. Your developer account should be assigned Manager (precedence 2) for full access during testing. Role Responsibilities​ Action Employee(Owner) Manager(Supervisor) Responsible Team(Reviewer) Create a new complaint ✅ Yes — — View own complaints ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Edit complaint description ✅ Yes (OPEN only) ✅ Yes — Assign responsible team — ✅ Yes — Move status → INPROCESS — ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Move status → ON HOLD — — ✅ Yes Move status → RESOLVED — ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Move status → CLOSED ✅ Yes ✅ Yes — Reopen a closed complaint ✅ Yes ✅ Yes — Add complaint items ✅ Yes (OPEN/INPROCESS) — — Add voice/comment records ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Upload attachments ✅ Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Escalate complaint ✅ Yes ✅ Yes — View all complaints (not just own) — ✅ Yes ✅ Yes (assigned) Entities to be Built​ Entity ID Primary Key Built in Session d_complaints complaint_id Session 1 d_complaint_item item_id Session 2 d_complaint_voices voice_id Session 2 d_complaints_attachment attachment_id Session 2 d_customers customer_id Session 2 d_resp_team emp_id Session 2 Complaint Status Flow​ The status lifecycle has 6 states. Each transition is triggered by a specific role: OPEN INPROCESS ON HOLD RESOLVED CLOSED REOPEN ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ Triggered by Employee Triggered by Manager / Responsible Team Triggered by Responsible Team Triggered by Responsible Team / Manager Triggered by Manager / Employee Triggered by Employee / Manager Status Badge Colour / Meaning OPEN Blue — complaint logged by Employee, awaiting Manager assignment INPROCESS Orange — Manager assigned responsible team; team working on it ON HOLD Purple — Responsible Team placed on hold pending information RESOLVED Green — Responsible Team marked as resolved CLOSED Grey — Manager confirmed resolution and closed the ticket REOPEN Red — Employee or Manager reopened a resolved/closed complaint 📘 Status Transition Rules OPEN → INPROCESS: only Manager can trigger (by assigning responsible_team).INPROCESS → ON HOLD / RESOLVED: only ResponsibleTeam can trigger.RESOLVED → CLOSED: only Manager can trigger.CLOSED → REOPEN: Employee or Manager can Relationships​ Relationship Detail d_complaints → d_complaint_item One Complaint → Many Items. d_complaint_item.ticket_id → d_complaints.complaint_id (Primary Relation — child of BO) d_complaints → d_customers.customer_id (Non-Primary Relation) Pages to be Built​ Screen ID Purpose p_home_page Home Page — summary tiles (Open count, Escalated count, Resolved Today), quick actions, and recent complaints list. Content adapts per role. p_complaints Complaint Management — list, search, and full detail view with tabs for items, voices, and attachments. Menu Structure​ Menu Item Screen Icon Visible to Complaints p_complaints sap-icon://customer-and-contacts All roles Naming Convention for This Training​ Item Convention App ID customer_complaints_<your_prid> e.g. customer_complaints_pr0045 Display Name Customer Complaints Application — <Your Name> Role 1 (Creator) Employee (precedence: 3) Role 2 (Assignor) Manager (precedence: 2) Role 3 (Resolver) ResponsibleTeam (precedence: 1) Test User (Employee) emp_<your_prid> e.g. emp_pr0045 Test User (Manager) mgr_<your_prid> e.g. mgr_pr0045 Test User (Resolver) res_<your_prid> e.g. res_pr0045 ⚠ Naming Rules App ID must be unique across the landscape — use your PRID to avoid collisions. Use only lowercase letters, numbers, and underscores. No spaces, hyphens, or special characters. The App ID cannot be changed after creation. ​ Part B — Workspace Hub: Users​ Reference: Workspace Hub 7.0 - User Guide Workspace Hub is an Admin Tool that focuses on managing applications and the application users. It is a versatile application that serves diverse purposes from user management to application management. Apart from that, this tool can also be used for modifying the already existing users and apps. Navigating to the Workspace Hub​ Workspace Hub menu will be visible for Users who are assigned as TESTER or DEVELOPER or SUPERADMIN for cockpit flavor. Step 1: Go to the menu options and select Workspace Hub. Step 2: The Workspace Hub contains the following Pages. What Is a User?​ A User is a platform-level account — a person who can log in to one or more applications. Users exist independently of applications. You create the person first, then assign them to applications with roles separately. The same user can have different roles in different applications. Creating a New User​ Create one test user to represent the end-user persona (emp01) throughout all sessions. 1 Navigate to Users In the Workspace Hub, click Users in the left navigation. The user list screen loads. 2 Click Create New User Click the create button in the toolbar. 3 Fill in User Details Complete all required fields as shown in the table below. Field What to enter Title Choose the title from dropdown (Mandatory) First Name Fill the first name (Mandatory) Last Name Fill the last name (Optional) Email A real or placeholder email address (Mandatory) Mobile Number used for OTP login if configured (Mandatory) Designation Fill the designation (Mandatory) User ID (Login ID) test_<your_prid> e.g. test_pr0045 BPID Choose bpid from dropdown (Mandatory) Authcode Choose authcode from dropdown (Mandatory) 4 Save the User Click Save. The user is created. Note the User ID — you will reference it when assigning this user to the application. Important — User Created ≠ User Has Access Creating a user only adds them to the platform's user directory. They cannot access any application until assigned to one with a specific role. You will complete that assignment in Part D of this session. If a user tries to log in before assignment, they will see error mentioning no applications assigned Refer Create User part from workspace hub manual for more information. Part C — Workspace Hub: Apps & Roles​ What Is an Application in Klobase?​ An application is a self-contained unit that holds all the metadata you build — entities, queries, pages, menus, and more. It is the primary organising structure of everything you will do in Sessions 2–8. Users are assigned to applications (with roles), not to individual Pages or features. Creating the Customer complaint Application​ 1 Navigate to Apps In the Workspace Hub, click Apps in the left navigation. 2 Click Create New App Click the Add button. The application creation form opens. 3 Fill in Application Details Complete the fields as shown in the table below. Field What to enter App ID Change the App ID according to the application App Name Same as app id Description (optional) Service Request Management training application 4 Save the Application Click Save. The app appears in the Apps list with Active status. Understanding Roles​ Roles control what a user can do inside the application. Procify has two categories: Role Type What it controls System Roles (built-in) MANAGER,DEVELOPER and TESTER— control access to dev tools (data studio,page builder, Workspace Hub, Private Node). Pre-built into the platform. Application Roles (custom) Roles you define inside your app. Control what users see and can do at runtime within your app's Pages and data. For this training, define single application role inside your app: Role Name Precedence Role Name DeliveryAgent 1 DeliveryAgent Role Precedence — Key Rule Precedence is a number. Lower number = higher priority. If a user has multiple roles, the one with the lowest precedence number takes effect at runtime. Delivery Admin(1) always overrides Delivery Agent(2) for a user assigned both roles. Your developer account will be Delivery Admin. The test user will be SRM_User. This lets you test both personas. Creating the DeliveryAgent Role​ 1 Open Your Application In the Apps list, click on srm_<prid> to open its detail screen. 2 Go to Roles & Users Click on the Roles & Users tab inside the application detail. 3 Create the DeliveryAgent Role In Application Roles, click Add. Role Name: DeliveryAgent.. Description: Field delivery personnel — can view and manage assigned deliveries. Click Save. 4 Verify Roles Are Listed Delivery Agents appear in the Application Roles list. Part D — Workspace Hub: App Assignment​ With the application created and roles defined, you now assign users to the application with their respective roles. Without this step, a user cannot see or open the application even with a valid platform account. Part D.1 — Team Groups: Bulk User Assignment​ What Is a Team Group?​ Assigning one test user at a time (as done in Part D) works fine for training, but it does not scale. Real projects onboard users in batches — a new hire cohort, an entire department, or a partner organisation that all needs the same app access on day one. Team Groups (labelled User collections inside the Workspace Hub screen) solve exactly this: they let you bundle a set of users once and assign the whole bundle to an application in a single step, instead of repeating the Part D steps per user. Team Groups are of two kinds: Individual Team Group — created automatically for every user the moment their account is created. Hidden by default (use the Show Individual checkbox to reveal them). Its only job is to let a newly created app be auto-assigned back to the user who created it. Group Team Group — created manually by an admin, and the one you will use for real onboarding work. With a Team Group, it becomes: 1 group with 25 members, linked once to an App Collection with 3 apps. Team Groups are filtered by the logged-in user’s Auth Codes and scoped to the current landscape — you will only see groups you are authorised to manage. Part E — understanding the importance of Procify​ Every application starts the same way: someone hands a developer a requirements document and says 'build this.' The Customer complaints Application Business Requirement Document (BRD) you read in Session 1 defines exactly what data needs to be stored — 3 data objects, their fields, and their relationships. The first job as a developer is to turn those definitions into a working database schema. Before opening any tool, it is worth understanding what that process looks like — and how much of it Procify eliminates. The rest of this part walks through the traditional process step by step, then shows exactly which steps the data studio replaces. What Is a Schema?​ 📘 Schema — The Blueprint of Your Application's Data A schema is the complete definition of the data your application stores: what tables exist, what columns each table has, what type of data each column holds, and how tables relate to each other. The schema is the foundation of every application. Without it, there is no database. Without a database, there is no data. Without data, there is no application. Building the schema is always the first development task after reading a BRD. Everything else — APIs, Pages, logic — is built on top of it. In our BRD, the schema is already defined in Section 4 (Entity Relationship Overview). The 4 entities, their properties, and their relationships are all there. Our job today is to implement that schema. The Traditional Way of Building a Schema​ 🏗 How developers build a schema without a low-code platform Step 1 — Write SQL scripts: A backend developer writes CREATE TABLE statements for each entity. For the Delivery table alone, that is 12 columns — each with its SQL data type, constraints, default values, and indexes. Step 2 — Write an ORM model: For every SQL table, the developer writes a model class in the backend language (Node.js/TypeScript, Python, Java). This class mirrors the database table and handles object-relational mapping. Step 3 — Write REST API endpoints: For each entity, the developer writes GET, POST, PUT, DELETE API handlers. Each handler validates input, maps it to the model, executes the database query, and returns the response. Step 4 — Write validation logic: For each property that has rules (mandatory, unique, min/max), the developer writes validation code — either in the model or in the API handler. Step 5 — Handle database migrations: Every time the schema changes (new property, renamed column), the developer writes a migration script to alter the existing tables without losing data. Step 6 — Test the API: The developer uses Postman or writes unit tests to verify each endpoint returns the correct data in the correct format. Repeat for all 4 entities. 🔴 The pain of the traditional approach Multiple files across multiple layers — SQL files, model files, API controller files, test files. A change to one field requires edits in 4–6 places. Context switching: a single developer must switch between SQL, backend language, API design, and test writing — each requiring a different mental mode. Time cost: 3–4 days of developer time before a single screen can be shown to a stakeholder. Repetition: most of this work is identical boilerplate — every entity needs the same pattern of SQL + ORM + CRUD APIs. Nothing creative, just repetitive. ​ The Procify Way​ ✅ How Procifyreplaces the traditional schema-building process In Klobase, all 6 traditional steps are replaced by a single tool: the data studio. You define the entity (name, type) → add properties (name, data type, key attributes) → click Update Schema. Done. The platform automatically generates: the database table (SQL step 1), the data access layer (ORM step 2), the REST API endpoints (step 3), basic validation from key attributes (step 4), and handles schema updates automatically (step 5). There are no separate files to keep in sync. The data studio is the single source of truth. Everything downstream — API, data validation, mobile sync — is derived from it automatically. Time with Klobase: the same 4 entities, all properties, schema live in the database — approximately 2 hours in this session. The developer's time is freed for the parts that actually require thinking: business logic, UI design, user experience. This is not an approximation. Let us make it concrete: Traditional Task data studio Replacement Write CREATE TABLE SQL for Delivery entity Create entity in data studio — choose type, add properties, click Save Write ORM model class (12 fields × 4 entities) Already done — properties ARE the model Write 16+ REST API endpoints Already done — fireQuery apis are available to fetch data Write validation for mandatory fields Check the Mandatory key attribute icon on the property and validation will be handled by platform. Write database migration script Click Update Schema again — the platform handles ALTER TABLE automatically Test APIs with Postman Use the built-in Test function in the data studio toolbar ​ The Traditional Way of Building a UI​ 🔴 Traditional screen development requires five separate layers 1. HTML / JSX template — the visual structure: list container, card component, placeholder slots for each field. 2. CSS / styling — card appearance, status badge colours, spacing, responsiveness for mobile and desktop. 3. API call — GET /complaints?user={currentUser.id} to fetch complaint records from the server. 4. State management (React state, Redux, etc.) — store the fetched array, handle loading state, handle error state, trigger re-renders when data changes. 5. Data binding — map each complaint object's fields to the template slots: {complaint.complaint_desc}, {complaint.priority}. Total: 3–5 files, 150–300 lines of code, for one list screen. Any change to one layer often requires changes to the others. The Procify Way — The Page Wizard & Page Builder​ ✅ The Page Builder replaces all five layers with a single metadata configuration In the Page Builder you configure the screen structure. The platform reads your configuration and generates the visual rendering, handles all data fetching, manages state automatically, applies your styling choices, and wires up the data bindings. This means: one tool, no files to keep in sync, no merge conflicts on screen structure, no state management code. The Page Wizard (used in this session) gives you a ready-made screen in minutes. Session 2 teaches you to build the same screen step-by-step so you understand every level of the hierarchy. Pages configured in the Page Builder render identically on both browser (web) and mobile (KloTouch) — no separate mobile codebase needed. B.3 — The Page Hierarchy (UI Editor 7.0 User Guide — Sections 3.0–7.0)​ Every screen in Klobase follows a strict 5-level hierarchy. This is the most important structural concept in UI development. Each level has a mandatory naming convention prefix: 📘 Five-Level Page Hierarchy Level 1 — PAGE (prefix: p_) The root container. Holds all layouts. Created first. One page can have multiple layouts (one per device type). At runtime, the platform picks the layout based on device: screencontainerdesktop, screencontainermobile, screencontainertab, screencontainerdefault. Level 2 — PAGE LAYOUT (prefix: pl_) Sits directly under the Page. Defines HOW the page areas are arranged. screenType options: stack, tab, two_column, object_page, grid_layout, hsplitter, vsplitter. Example: pl_complaints_desk (two column layout for desktop). Level 3 — PAGE AREA (prefix: pa_) A logical sub-container inside the layout. Can itself have a screenType (tab, stack, splitter). Sections are assigned to page areas to determine WHERE they render. Example: pa_complaints (list area), pa_complaint_details (detail area). Level 4 — SECTION (prefix: s_) The rendering unit. screenType determines HOW it displays data. Types: search, cardlist, card, form, grid, tree, timeline, map, calendar. Must be assigned to a Page Area to appear in the UI. Example: s_search (search), s_complaints (grid), s_detail_header (form). Level 5 — CONTROLS Individual fields, buttons, labels, icons bound to entity properties. Added via: right-click section → New → Controls, OR drag from unused TransNode properties. Section screenType Renders As search Filter bar with Close / Reset / Search buttons. Auto-generates the search toolbar. cardlist List of records as card rows — one card per record. Good for mobile and compact lists. grid Tabular list with column headers and rows. Supports sort, filter, group-by per column. form Detail form layout. Each control renders as a labelled input field. card Single entity rendered as a CSS grid card. One record only. tab Used on Page Areas to group child sections as tabs. showTitle must be true for tab labels. tree Hierarchical tree display for nested data. B.4 — Page Data Model (TransNodes) — Concept​ The Page Data Model defines the data available to a screen. Every section and control that displays data must be bound to a TransNode. A TransNode is a “data pipe” — it fetches entity records from the database and makes them available to sections and controls on the page. Node Type Fetches EntitySet A LIST of records. Use for search sections, grids, card lists. Suffix convention: _list. Example: d_complaints_list Entity ONE record (the currently selected record). Use for detail forms. Suffix convention: _detail. Example: d_complaints_detail Query Records from a kloQuery with WHERE conditions, joins, sorting. Suffix convention: _query. Other Non-standard / custom use cases. 📘 Fold From — The Critical Link Between List and Detail When you create d_complaints_detail (Entity type) and set its “Fold From” = d_complaints_list, the platform automatically loads the selected record’s data into d_complaints_detail whenever the user clicks a row in the list. This is the mechanism that connects list → detail. Without Fold From: the detail section will always be empty. With Fold From: clicking any complaint row in the list instantly populates the detail form. You can drag and drop controls within the section to align the controls. 📸 Final Output — After Creating s_search Once s_search is created with all controls and you click Show Full Preview, you will see the search filter bar rendered at the top of the screen exactly as shown below. Expected output: s_search renders the Employee Complaints filter bar with all fields — Ticket Id, Status, Complaint Type, Escalated checkbox, Employee Category, Priority, Nature of Complaint, Actual TAT, and Standard TAT. Close / Reset / Search buttons are auto-generated by the search scr eenType. 📸 Tree View — How s_search Looks in the Page Builder Tree After adding all controls, s_search in the tree should look like the screenshot below. Each control is listed under the section with its entity property binding. Page Builder tree showing pa_complaints → s_search with all controls: ticket_id, desc, customer_id, responsible_tea, priority, s_status, is_escalated, cust_category_lbl, cust_category, cust_type_lbl, cust_type, complaint_type, raised_by, state, nature_of_compl, actual_tat, standard_tat B.9.2 — Creating the Complaints List Section (s_complaints)​ The grid section renders complaint records as rows with sortable, filterable columns. Per UI Editor 7.0 Guide (Section 6.2 — Grid): For desktop view, section screenType should be “grid”. Add a conf_grid000 config node for grid behaviour settings. 1 Right-click pa_complaints → New → Section. Rename: s_complaints. 2 In the Detail panel, set screenType = grid. 3 Set TransNode path = list. 4 Right-click pa_complaints → New → Assign → select s_complaints (below s_search). Save. 5 Add controls from d_complaints_list TransNode unused properties: ticket_id (set the control type as m.link and add press event with function as ‘navTo’(Fill the sunscreen id as detail page area) ), customer_id, priority, s_status, planned_res_dat, closed_on, sales_manager. 6 Right-click s_complaints → New → Config → rename: conf_grid000. This config node stores grid behaviour properties. 7 Right-click s_complaints → New → Toolbar. Add Add and Delete buttons in the toolbar detail. 8 Arrange the controls in s_complaints by using drag and drop feature inside section 9 Save. 📸 Final Output — After Creating s_complaint Once s_complaints is created with all controls and you click Show Full Preview, you will see the complaints list rendered below search section You can notice that the screen we created is not the same in the provided screenshot. Complaint_id contains id-desc Status has color Grid is occupying full screen Pont 1 & 2 will be achieved in the upcoming sessions. Rename: pa_comp_details. 2 In the Detail panel, set screenType = default. Right-click pa_comp_details → New → Section for each. Set each to screenType = form Set TransNode = detail for form sections. 5 Set each section’s title property — this becomes the tab label visible at runtime. 5 Assign all 4 sections to pa_comp_details in the correct sequence. documents.t: By the end of this session, you will be able to: Understand what Entity Relations are and create Primary and Non-Primary (Aggregated) relations between entities. Understand what Object Types are, why they are needed, and configure complaint type classifications for d_complaints. Configure Status and Status Groups to represent the complaint lifecycle (OPEN → INPROCESS → ON HOLD → RESOLVED → CLOSED → REOPEN). Set up an ID Series for complaint_id to auto-generate readable complaint numbers (e.g. CMP-00001). Update the p_complaints UI to reflect the new entity configuration — making the complaint_type, status, and complaint_id fields work correctly in the page. 📘 What This Session Builds On Session 1 created the application, roles, users, and d_complaints entity with raw properties. Session 2 created the remaining 5 entities and built the full p_complaints page step by step. Session 3 enriches the d_complaints entity with the platform features that turn raw fields into intelligent, lifecycle-aware data. After Session 3, the complaint_id will auto-generate, the status dropdown will show the correct lifecycle values, and complaint_type will be classified. Without a relation defined in the BOL Editor, the platform has no way to automatically load child records when a parent record is selected — and no way to bundle the BO for save/delete operations. There are two types of relations in Klobase: Relation Type What It Means Primary Relation Tight parent-child bond WITHIN the same Business Object (BO). A child entity is dependent on the parent. Prefixed pr_. Used for d_complaint_item, d_complaint_voices, d_complaints_attachment — all children of d_complaints. Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relation Looser link BETWEEN BOs. Used to reference standalone master entities. Prefixed r_. Used for d_customers and d_resp_team which are independent master entities. 📘 Why Relations Matter in the UI When a relation is defined and referenced in a TransNode in the Page Builder, the platform automatically fetches the child/linked entity records when the parent record is loaded. Without a relation, you would have to write manual queries and wire up the data fetch yourself. The TransNode type 'Relation' in the Page Data Model uses the relation name defined here — this is why naming the relation correctly matters. Naming convention (from BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Best Practices): pr_ prefix for primary relations, r_ prefix for associated/aggregated relations. Always lowercase. A.2 — Relations to Create for d_complaints​ You will create 5 relations on the d_complaints root entity — one for each related entity. Relation ID Type Return Entity Cardinality r_complaint_item Non-Primary (Aggregated) d_complaint_item 1:n (One complaint → Many items) r_complaint_voices Non-Primary (Aggregated) d_complaint_voices 1:n (One complaint → Many voices) r_complaint_attach Non-Primary (Aggregated) d_complaints_attachment 1:n (One complaint → Many attachments) r_customer Non-Primary (Aggregated) d_customers 1:1 (One complaint has one customer) r_resp_team Non-Primary (Aggregated) d_resp_team 1:1 (One complaint has one responsible team member) A.3 — Step-by-Step: Creating a Primary Relation​ Primary Relation will be automatically created with the creation of child entity and requires no manual action A.4 — Step-by-Step: Creating a Non-Primary (Aggregated) Relation​ Non-primary relations link d_complaints to standalone master entities (d_customers and d_resp_team). Follow these steps for r_customer # Action Detail 1 d_complaints Relations tab click d_complaints in the tree and go back to the Relations tab. 2 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon to add a new relation row. 3 Fill Relation Details Relation Name: r_customer 4 Configure Mapping Click Mapping. Add: Source Property = customer_id 5 Save Click Save. 💡 Mapping Type — BOTH Explained ON CREATE: When a new d_complaint_item is created under a d_complaints parent, the platform automatically copies the complaint_id value into the ticket_id field of the new item. You never have to set this manually. ON QUERY: When you query d_complaint_item records for a given complaint, the platform uses ticket_id = complaint_id as the WHERE condition automatically. BOTH: Use this for standard parent-child relations — it handles both the create and the fetch scenarios. Now repeat the same steps to create the remaining relations: Relation ID Return Entity Mapping (Source → Target) r_complaint_voices d_complaint_voices complaint_id → ticket_id r_complaint_items d_complaint_item complaint_id → ticket_id r_complaint_attach d_complaints_attachment complaint_id → complaint_id r_resp_team d_resp_team responsible_team → emp_id Part B — Configuring Object Types for d_complaints​ B.1 — What Is an Object Type?​ In Klobase, an Object Type (stored in the system property s_object_type) is a classification that tags each record as belonging to a specific type. Object Types serve two important purposes: They enable role-based visibility: a button or field can be made visible/editable only for a specific role AND a specific object type combination. This is used for screen behavior in Session 7. They allow ID Series to be object-type-specific: a different number series prefix can be applied per object type — for example, complaints created by Maventic employees might use a different prefix than those created by Procify employees. 📘 Object Type vs Object Group Object Group is a container that groups related Object Types together. The group is used as the filter boundary. Object Type is the actual tag applied to individual records (e.g. MAVENTIC, PROCIFY). Every Object Type must belong to exactly one Object Group. For the Customer Complaints application: Object Group = company_types Object Types = MAVENTIC, PROCIFY Best Practice (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide): Always maintain an Object Group to group types — the same group can be used in default filters based on users. B.2 — Object Types for d_complaints​ Object Type ID Description MAVENTIC Complaints created by Maventic employees PROCIFY Complaints created by Procify employees B.3 — Step-by-Step: Creating Object Group and Object Types​ # Action Detail 1 Go to Object Type tab Select d_complaints in the tree. Click the Object Type tab in the Detail panel. The tab shows two sections: the upper section for Object Types 2 Open Object Group dialog In the Object Type section, click the dialog icon next to the Object Group field to open the Object Group management dialog. 3 Create Object Group In the Object Group dialog, click Add. Fill in: Object Group ID: complaint_types 4 Close dialog Click Cancel / Close on the Object Group dialog to return to the Object Type tab. 5 Add first Object Type Fill: Object Type: MAVENTIC 6 Add remaining types Repeat Add for: PROCIFY — under Object Group: complaint_types. Click Save after all are added. 7 Verify All Object Types appear in the list, all with Object Group: complaint_types. ​ After adding the object type to differentiate complaints based on company is only half in order to achieve difference in complaint_id based on company another part is pending which is configuring ID Series based on object_type. Part C — Setting Up ID Series for Auto-Numbering​ D.1 — What Is an ID Series?​ An ID Series is a platform-managed counter that automatically generates primary key values when a new record is created. Without an ID Series on complaint_id, a developer would need to generate unique IDs manually — which is error-prone and cannot produce readable, formatted numbers like CMP-00001. ID Series Type Description Auto Number Returns an incrementing number. Combined with a Prefix pattern to produce CMP-00001, CMP-00002, etc. GUID Returns a 32-character UUID. Good for distributed offline scenarios. Not human-readable. None No auto-generation. The developer or rule must set the key manually. D.2 — ID Series to Configure​ Property Type Company Pattern/Prefix Start From complaint_id Auto Number PROCIFY Prefix: P- (generates P-00001) 1 complaint_id Auto Number MAVENTIC Prefix: M - (generates M-00001) 1 D.3 — Step-by-Step: Creating the ID Series​ # Action Detail 1 Select d_complaints In the Data Studio tree, click on d_complaints. 2 Go to Properties tab Click the Properties tab in the Detail panel. Locate the complaint_id property row. 3 Open ID Series Click the navigation right arrow (→) at the end of the complaint_id row. The ID Series dialog opens for this property. 4 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon in the ID Series dialog. A new entry row appears. 5 Fill ID Series details ID: idp_complaint 6 Click Add Click the Add (+) icon in the ID Series dialog. A new entry row appears. 7 Fill ID Series details ID: idm_complaint 8 Close dialog Click Close on the dialog. The ID Series entry is saved. 9 Save Click Save in the Data Studio toolbar. The complaint_id property now has an ID Series configured. 📘 ID Series Fields Reference (BOL Editor 7.0 User Guide — Section 3.0.1 Creating ID Series) ID: Unique ID of the series. Naming convention: id_ prefix, all lowercase. Example: id_complaint. Type: Auto Number = incremental counter. Most common for business records. From: Starting number for the series. Use 1 to start from P-00001. Prefix: Text prepended before the number. P- produces P-1, P-2, etc. Chunk Size: Default 100. The server pre-allocates this many IDs per session (important for offline apps). Scope: Global (default) — one counter shared across all users and tenants. Pattern: Can be used to produce complex formats. For simple prefix + number, just use the Prefix field. D.4 — Testing the ID Series​ # Action Detail 1 Open Data Browser With d_complaints selected, click Test in the toolbar. The Data Browser opens. 2 Create a new record Click Add (+ Execute → Add → select object_type). Leave complaint_id blank — the platform will fill it. 3 Fill minimal fields complaint_desc: Test auto-number 4 Verify The complaint_id column should show P-00001 for Procify and M-0001 for Maventic (or the next available number). If it shows a blank or an error, revisit the ID Series configuration. Part C — Configuring Status and Status Groups​ C.1 — What Is Status in Klobase?​ The system property s_status represents the current state of a complaint record. The Status tab in the Data Studio lets you define the allowed values for s_status and group them into Status Groups. Status Groups are named collections of statuses. They are used in Vienable (Session 7) to control screen behaviour: for example, the Edit button is visible only when s_status is in the OPEN_GROUP, and the Assign Team button is visible only when s_status is in the INPROCESS_GROUP. 📘 Status Lifecycle for Customer Complaints The complaint lifecycle defined in the BRD has 6 states: OPEN → INPROCESS → ON_HOLD / RESOLVED → CLOSED / REOPEN Each status transition is triggered by a specific role (defined in the Role Responsibility matrix from Session 1 Part A). In this session you define the status values and groups. The actual UI enforcement of transitions using Vienable happens in Session 7. C.2 — Status Values and Groups to Configure​ Status ID Short Label Status Group Triggered By OPEN Open OPEN Auto-set on complaint creation by Employee INPROCESS In Process INPROCESS Manager assigns responsible_team ON_HOLD On Hold INPROCESS Responsible Team puts on hold RESOLVED Resolved ACCEPTED Responsible Team / Manager marks resolved CLOSED Closed COMPLETED Manager confirms resolution and closes REOPEN Re-Opened OPEN Employee or Manager reopens a closed complaint C.3 — Step-by-Step: Adding Status Values​ # Action Detail 1 Go to Status tab Select d_complaints in the tree. Click the Status tab in the Detail panel. 2 Enable Switch on the status and click save and edit 3 Add OPEN status Click the Add Record(+) icon. Fill: Status: OPEN 4 Add remaining statuses Repeat Add for each status: INPROCESS (In Process), ON_HOLD (On Hold), RESOLVED (Resolved), CLOSED (Closed), REOPEN (Re-Opened) for PROCIFY. Click Save after all are added. Repeat for MAVENTIC Repeat the Action 3 and 4 for object_type maventic as well. 4 Verify list All 12 status values appear in the status list. 💡 Why Status Groups Are Important for This Application Session 7 will use these groups to configure Vienable on buttons and fields. Example: The 'Edit' button will be configured as: Visible only when s_status_group = OPEN_GROUP. Example: The 'Assign Team' button will be: Visible only when s_status_group = OPEN_GROUP and Role = Manager. Without the groups defined now, the Vienable configuration in Session 7 cannot be done. Part E — Updating the UI to Reflect Entity Configuration​ Now that d_complaints has Relations, Object Types, Status values, and an ID Series configured, the p_complaints page must be updated to expose and use these configurations. In this part you will: Add Relation-based TransNodes to p_complaints for d_complaint_item, d_complaint_voices, and d_complaints_attachment. Connect the s_complaint_item grid (already in the pa_comp_details tab from Session 2) to the d_complaint_item relation TransNode. Verify the complaint_id field auto-populates from the ID Series. Verify the s_status field on the search section and the detail form is bound and showing the correct status values. 📘 Why the UI Needs to Be Updated When you added Relations in Part A, the platform can now automatically fetch child records. But the Page Builder still needs to be told WHICH TransNode to use to access that relation data. A Relation-type TransNode in the Page Data Model references the relation name (pr_complaint_item) and automatically joins child records to the active parent complaint record. The complaint_id field in the form section can now be set to read-only since the ID Series will fill it — the user should not manually enter a complaint ID. E.1 — Add Relation TransNodes to the Page Data Model​ # Action Detail 1 Open Page Builder Navigate to Design Studio → Page Builder. Select customer_complaints_<prid>. Click the Edit icon to enable edit mode. 2 Select p_complaints Click p_complaints in the tree. Open the Page Data Model panel (right-side tab). 3 Review existing TransNodes You should see: search (Query), list (EntitySet / Transfer&Link from search), detail (Entity / Transfer&Link from list). These were created in Session 2. 4 Add complaint item TransNode Click the detail transnode → click + icon available next to r_complaint_item in unused properties. Fill: Path: complaint_items 6 Repeat Repeat Action 4 for relation voices, attachments 7 Save Click Save. E.2 — Wire the s_complaint_item Section to the Relation TransNode​ Need to create a s_complaint_item, s_complaint_voices, s_complaint_attachments section with screen_type as grid and bind with respective transnode. # Action Detail 1 Create s_complaint_item Right-click pa_complaint_details → new → section → right click section → rename : s_complaint_item 3 Mark type as section Add type = section for s_complaint_items layout 2 Open Detail panel Click s_complaint_item to open its Detail properties on the right. And fil title = items 3 Set TransNode path In the TransNode/Path field, set: complaint_items. This references the relation TransNode created in E.1 Step 4. 4 Add controls Right-click s_complaint_item → New → Controls. Add: item_id, product, issue_observed. Or drag from Page Data Model → d_complaint_item → Unused Properties. 5 Set screen type Confirm s_complaint_item screenType = grid. Set showTitle = true so the tab label 'Complaint Items' is visible. 6 Add Section Toolbar Right click on s_complaint_item → New → Toolbar Add and Delete buttons will be added to section if not enable showAdd and showDelete properties as true 7 Add Save Button Right click on the section toolbar → Action/Items → update text → add press event and select save from vh. 8 Add config Right click- s_complaint_item → new → config Add visibleRowCountMode = Fixed Repeat the same for s_complaint_voices and s_complaint_attachments as well with respective transnodes. E.4 — Verify s_status in Search and Detail Sections​ The s_status field is a system property. Now that Status values are configured in the BOL Editor (Part C), the status dropdown in the search section and detail form will automatically render the configured values (OPEN, INPROCESS, ON_HOLD, RESOLVED, CLOSED, REOPEN). # Action Detail 1 Click Show Full Preview Add the property in s_search and s_complaint_detail and In the Page Builder, click Show Full Preview to load live data. 2 Verify s_status in search bar In the search filter bar, click the Status dropdown. Verify the 6 status values appear: OPEN, INPROCESS, ON_HOLD, RESOLVED, CLOSED, REOPEN. 3 Click a complaint row Select any complaint record from the list. The detail area loads. 4 Verify complaint_id 1. For creating complaints with object_type enable showAddWithObjectType option for s_complaint_list section toolbar. 2. The complaint_id field should show the P-00001 or M-0001 format based on object_type (or different if the test record was created before the ID Series was set up — create a new record to confirm). 5 Verify Complaint Items tab Click the Complaint Items tab in the pa_comp_details area. If the selected complaint has items, they should appear in the grid. The tab was empty in Session 2 — it should now have a data source.

Verify the voice record is linked to the complaint via the ticket_id field.
